pl-l3d21c2-d1e117.summary: States that when the soul departed Christ's flesh died, and so Christ died: as God is said to have died when the man died, the man is said to have died when the flesh died. Because the flesh united to the Word died, God is said to have died; because flesh and soul felt pain, God is said to have suffered, though the divinity was free from all pain.
claims: Christ died because his flesh died when the soul departed.
God is said to die and suffer because of the flesh and soul united to him.
The divinity was free from all pain.

pl-l3d21c2-d1e123.summary: Quotes Augustine: the Word was crucified without being changed into man; through what was man, God died, and through what was God, the man rose. Whatever the man suffered cannot be said not to be suffered by God, as you suffer injury if your garment is torn, though you are not your garment; yet the Word could neither die nor be corrupted nor changed, and suffered only in the flesh.
claims: Whatever the flesh united to the Word suffers, God is said to suffer.
The Word suffered only in the flesh, remaining unchangeable.

pl-l3d21c2-d1e132.summary: Quotes Ambrose: the Word remaining in the flesh referred the flesh's suffering to itself by reason of assuming the body, so that it was said to suffer. Lombard draws out that God is said to have suffered or died not because he felt death as God, but because the flesh united to him died.
claims: God is said to suffer because his flesh suffered, not because he felt death as God.

pl-l3d21c2-d1e148.summary: Cites, in line with this reasoning, an anathema attributed to Augustine against anyone who says and believes that God the Son of God suffered.
claims: It is anathema to hold that the Son of God suffered as God.

pl-l3d21c2-d1e157.summary: Gives the reason for that anathema, which shows how to read it: it targets anyone who says that the Son of God as God felt pain in the passion, rather than the flesh with the soul he assumed.
claims: The anathema concerns attributing pain to the divinity itself.

pl-l3d21c2-d1e163.summary: Concludes that one may soundly say God died and did not die, the Son of God suffered and did not suffer, the Word was crucified and was not crucified: he suffered according to one nature and was impassible according to the other.
claims: Contrary predications of Christ are both true, referred to different natures.

pl-l3d21c2-d1e166.summary: Confirms with Ambrose: the common faith holds that Christ, Son of God and born of the Virgin, is one of twin natures, like the prophet's giant. The same one suffered and did not suffer, died and did not die, rose and did not rise: he rose according to the flesh that had died, not according to the Word that always remained with God.
claims: The same Christ suffered and did not suffer according to different natures.
Christ rose according to the flesh, not according to the Word.

pl-l3d21c2.summary: Explains in what sense God is said to have died and suffered. When the soul departed, Christ's flesh died and so Christ died; because the flesh united to the Word died, God is said to have died, and because the flesh and soul united to him felt pain, God is said to have suffered, though the divinity was untouched by pain. Augustine's analogy of a torn garment and Ambrose confirm this; Augustine's anathema on saying that God the Son suffered is aimed at those who say he felt pain in his divinity. God therefore died and did not die, suffered and did not suffer, in one nature and not the other.
claims: God is said to have died because the flesh united to the Word died.
God is said to have suffered because the soul and flesh united to him felt pain.
Christ suffered according to one nature and was impassible according to the other.
